who: People who cannot shake or tilt a device
takeaways: If moving the device, such as shaking or tilting, or moving in front of a camera triggers an action, an on-screen control does the same thing.
People can also turn the motion response off, so a tremor or a bus ride does not trigger it by accident.
Exceptions: the motion is essential, like a step counter, or it works through an accessibility-supported interface.
This is about motion as input. Animation that moves on screen is 2.3.3 and 2.2.2.
failures: Shake to undo with no undo button
Tilt to scroll with no way to turn it off
A “wave to continue” camera gesture as the only option
check: List every feature that reacts to device or body motion.
Find the button or control that does the same thing.
Find the setting that turns the motion response off.

quiz.question: Your app adds shake to report a bug. What else does it need?
options: A “Report a bug” button, plus a setting to turn shake off
A firmer shake threshold to avoid accidents
quiz.why: Some people cannot shake a phone, and others shake it without meaning to. The button covers the first group and the off switch covers the second.

spec: For each motion feature, name the on-screen control that does the same thing.
Specify where the setting to disable motion lives, and its default.
Mark any motion you treat as essential, and why.
review: What happens if this phone is clamped to a wheelchair?
Could this fire by accident in someone’s pocket or on a bus?
Where is the switch to turn this off?
tradeoff: Motion features feel playful and save screen space. Keep them as extras, never the only route, and make turning them off one clear setting.
system: Pair every motion trigger with a standard button and a shared “Motion controls” setting.
pitch: Shake and tilt are delightful until your phone is bolted to a wheelchair. A button and an off switch keep the delight without locking anyone out.
